name: Third Council of Constantinople
summary: The council that condemned monothelitism, the teaching that Christ had only one will, and anathematized past patriarchs and Pope Honorius I.
place: Constantinople (the domed hall, or Trullo, of the imperial palace)

background.text: In the 630s Patriarch Sergius of Constantinople and Emperor Heraclius promoted the formula of one 'energy' and then one will in Christ to reconcile the opponents of Chalcedon. Heraclius's Ekthesis (638) imposed it, and Pope Honorius I had written approvingly of 'one will'.

Constans II's Typos (648) forbade all discussion of the issue. Pope Martin I and Maximus the Confessor condemned monothelitism at the Lateran Synod of 649, and both were then arrested and punished by the emperor.
Constantine IV, wanting peace with Rome after the Arab conquests had taken the provinces monothelitism was meant to win over, asked Pope Agatho for delegates and summoned a council.

happened.text: Constantine IV presided over many of the 18 sessions in person; attendance grew from fewer than 50 to about 150 bishops.
The council accepted Pope Agatho's letter, which taught two wills in Christ, as it had accepted Leo's Tome at Chalcedon.
Macarius of Antioch defended one will, refused to give way, and was deposed during the council.
It defined that Christ has two natural wills and two natural operations, divine and human, the human will following and subject to the divine.

participants.name: Agatho
participants.role: Bishop of Rome; his letter set out the teaching adopted

participants.name: Macarius of Antioch
participants.role: Patriarch; defended monothelitism and was deposed

outcomes.text: Pope Leo II confirmed the council in 682, including the condemnation of Honorius, whom he described as having allowed the faith to be stained by not suppressing heresy.
The condemnation of a pope became a central argument in the debate over papal infallibility at the First Vatican Council (1870).
Monothelitism was briefly revived by Emperor Philippikos (711–713) and lasted longer among the Maronites of Lebanon, who later entered communion with Rome.

condemnations.authority: Council of bishops under Constantine IV
condemnations.reason: Patriarchs Sergius, Pyrrhus, Paul, and Peter of Constantinople, Cyrus of Alexandria, and Theodore of Pharan anathematized posthumously as monothelites

condemnations.authority: Council of bishops under Constantine IV
condemnations.reason: Pope Honorius I (d. 638) anathematized posthumously for following Sergius's opinions
condemnations.status: Confirmed by Pope Leo II (682); Catholic theologians debate whether it touched his teaching authority

condemnations.authority: Council of bishops under Constantine IV
condemnations.reason: Macarius of Antioch and his disciple Stephen deposed and anathematized for monothelitism

persecution_note: The council itself deposed Macarius and sent him to Rome for confinement. The harshest persecution in the controversy came before it, under the monothelite emperor Constans II.

persecution.title: Deposition and confinement of Macarius of Antioch
persecution.summary: After his deposition, the emperor sent Macarius and his followers to Rome, where Pope Leo II placed them in monasteries.

persecution.title: Arrest and exile of Pope Martin I (before the council)
persecution.summary: On Constans II's orders the exarch Theodore Calliopas arrested Martin in Rome in June 653. He was taken to Constantinople, tried for treason, publicly humiliated, and exiled to Cherson in Crimea.

responsible.name: Theodore Calliopas
responsible.role: Exarch of Ravenna; made the arrest

persecution.outcome: Died in exile in 655; venerated as a martyr by Catholic and Orthodox churches.

persecution.title: Trials and mutilation of Maximus the Confessor (before the council)
persecution.summary: Maximus was arrested with Martin, tried and exiled, and tried again in 662 by a synod in Constantinople. His tongue and right hand were cut off so that he could no longer speak or write against monothelitism, and he was exiled to Lazica in the Caucasus.
persecution.outcome: Died in exile in Lazica on 13 August 662; the 681 council vindicated his teaching.
